tags/economics/finance/index.title: #finance
tags/economics/finance/index.content: I spent the start of my career in data engineering at fintech companies. While it doesn’t come up as much in my day-to-day at this point, related notes will be tagged here when they come up.

tags/economics/index.title: #economics
tags/economics/index.content:
Economics is where I spent my actual undergraduate career, and I worked as a fintech data analyst and engineer in the early years of my career. While I work professionally as a more general software engineer at this point, I still like to keep up with more econometrics and policy-focused topics.
When I was studying economics, most of my academic focus was in market design and non-monetary systems like:

Efficient task delegation, which — very helpfully — carries over to efficiencies in distributed computing and project management;
Matchmaking algorithms; and
Incentive structures in markets where monetary compensation is a secondary concern, such as the open-source software (OSS) ecosystem.

tags/economics/markets/index.title: #markets
tags/economics/markets/index.content: The #markets tag is dedicated to notes specifically around the design, structure, and analysis of (non-financial) markets.

tags/economics/policy/index.title: #economics/policy
tags/economics/policy/index.content: Eventually the rubber has to hit the road, and research has to become application. When it comes to economics, this is often in the form of public policy. When any notes or research relate to this policy, they’ll be tagged here.

tags/economics/strategy/index.title: #strategy
tags/economics/strategy/index.content: Much of my academic time in economics was spent evaluating how actors, both people and companies, evaluate and make decisions. Since I now work at companies — what a concept! — notes related to decision-making and resource allocations, especially around task delegation and project management, will be tagged here.

tags/engineering/ai/index.title: #ai
tags/engineering/ai/index.content: The engineering/ai tag contains notes and content related to AI systems — it’s distinctly more LLM- and tooling-oriented than, say, data, which focuses more on data science and engineering.

tags/engineering/bio/index.title: #bio
tags/engineering/bio/index.content: Through my partner’s career in biomedical engineering, I’m tangentially aware of (and have attended quite a few thesis defense sessions) related to biomedical engineering. Notes related to these types of sessions, as well as other things in the space that happen to crop up, are tagged here.

tags/engineering/data/index.title: #data
tags/engineering/data/index.content: One of the things that lights my brain up is bring able to process, analyze, and visualize cool datasets. I’ve been incredibly fortunate to be able to make a living out of that. This tag is a catch-all for projects related to data processing, statistics, and data engineering.

tags/engineering/devops/index.title: #devops
tags/engineering/devops/index.content: DevOps is one of those roles that you just kinda… fall into. It’s nice, for both my own benefit and for the benefit of the folks I work with, to be able to automate away busywork. Where I can make guides and software publicly available, those will be tagged here.

tags/engineering/frontend/index.title: #frontend
tags/engineering/frontend/index.content:
I’m really more of a backend, DevOps, and data person. A lot of my frontend experience is in build systems for TypeScript applications — things like wrangling (P)NPM dependencies and build times, orchestration via NX, and mobile app deployments through Fastlane.
These posts will be a mixture of actual web development (like this site, for example), but may be co-opted with data visualizations if they’re particularly pretty.

tags/engineering/index.title: #engineering
tags/engineering/index.content: My personal projects and professional focus has been primarily in software engineering. Being able to make things that help people, including myself, accomplish more is a joy that lights up my brain.

tags/engineering/languages/csharp/index.title: #csharp
tags/engineering/languages/csharp/index.content:
I had done a few projects in C# back in college, especially through trying my hand at trying my hand at broader game development. That has picked up substantially since starting a dayjob at a C# and TypeScript shop.
This page is for all available posts related, either directly or indirectly, to my OSS C# development.

tags/engineering/languages/index.title: #languages
tags/engineering/languages/index.content:
I’m certainly not a person who has strong opinions about programming languages. My personal and professional decision graph around language choice is:
flowchart TD
    A[What language<br/>are you most familiar with?] --> B{Will it get<br/>the job done?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Use that language.]
    B -->|No| D[Repeat.]
    D --> A

That said, I do break out languages according to the task:

























The JobThe LanguagesApplication development.NET and TypeScript (stack used for my day job)Data science and engineeringPython and/or .NET (via Flowthru)Game developmentTypeScript, .NET, and LuaWeb developmentTypeScript and/or .NET (via Blazor)

tags/engineering/languages/lua/index.title: #lua
tags/engineering/languages/lua/index.content: Lua is a language that I rarely use anymore — that chunk of my development has largely switched over to TypeScript — but it does still come up from time to time. When the occasions arise, those posts will be tagged here.

tags/engineering/languages/python/index.title: #python
tags/engineering/languages/python/index.content: For much of my early career, I worked primarily in Python for data science, analysis, and engineering. While I don’t use it as much anymore, it’s a handy tool for quick prototyping and data projects, especially in AI, LLM, and machine learning projects. It’ll come up from time to time, and those projects will show up here.

tags/engineering/languages/scratch/index.title: #scratch
tags/engineering/languages/scratch/index.content: Scratch is a massively beginner-friendly code editor. Back in my undergrad at the University of Utah, I worked a couple of summers as a programming camp instructor. I doubt it’ll come up often, but when it does, you’ll find those posts marked here.

tags/engineering/languages/typescript/in.title: #typescript
tags/engineering/languages/typescript/in.content: I’ve never been a bona-fide Typescript Developer™, but through my work, I’ve become well-acquainted with the stack for deployment and build orchestration. While I’m not a frontend engineer by trade, it’ll come up a bit as new projects requiring frontends crop up, and in DevOps posts that may be helpful enough to publish.

tags/horticulture/index.title: #horticulture
tags/horticulture/index.content:
Horticulture is a term I started using during the Season of Rhythm, specifically picked up from the term digital gardening.
Most of the time, horticulture relates to maintaining systems like this blog, along with other personal systems that either maintain my ability to manage my own life, and, in turn, might require their own maintenance over time.

tags/horticulture/seasons/index.title: #seasons
tags/horticulture/seasons/index.content: There’s always something I need to work on in my life. I’ve started labelling periods of time with seasons — specific things I, personally, want to focus on improving. While most of the posts will be private, some public posts will be a result of the season and tagged accordingly.

tags/horticulture/seasons/rhythm/index.title: #rhythm
tags/horticulture/seasons/rhythm/index.content:
The Season of Rhythm is my first season, when I adopted a personal practice of trying to focus blocks of time around specific tasks. Season of Rhythm is focused around developing a strong habits and routines, which I need to redevelop after graduating from my undergraduate and starting full-time remote work. It’s also the start of digital gardening
Season of Rhythm has been wrapped up, and followed by the Season of Systems.

tags/horticulture/seasons/systems/index.title: #systems
tags/horticulture/seasons/systems/index.content: The Season of Systems is the (long overdue) follow-up to Season of Rhythm. A lot of this season is focused around developing both personal systems — organizing longer-running tasks, refining how I collect everything I need to do on a day-to-day and week-to-week basis — along with professional systems for staying on top of the many AI systems that have grown out over the past year.

tags/private/index.title: #private
tags/private/index.content:
In the era of AI consuming everything publicly available on the Internet, I made a call during my Season of Systems to take some of the more personal notes — primarily the periodic notes, like dailies and weeklies — private. I keep the metadata, like tags and links, available. However, most of them are stashed away separate from this site and repository.
If you do see a private note that catches your eye, and you’d like to know more about it, you’re absolutely welcome to reach out. If it’s not terribly sensitive, I’d be happy to chat about it!

tags/projects/dayjob/index.title: #dayjob
tags/projects/dayjob/index.content:
As part of my daily gardening, I write brief notes about tasks to get done at my day job. The vast majority of these notes will be private, except when taking notes on other publicly-available materials that I am recommended, or assigned to annotate, at work.
If you do have questions about my daily work, my resume has publicly-available information about broad strokes responsibilities. You’re also welcome to contact me — if it’s something I’m clear to talk about, I’m happy to chat!

tags/projects/flowthru/index.title: #flowthru
tags/projects/flowthru/index.content:
A data engineering project that attempts to use a Kedro-style API surface to create data pipelines in .NET that will catch errors at compile time, instead of at runtime.
The first production project using Flowthru is the analysis portions of MagicAtlas.
Full documentation lives at flowthru.chaoticgood.computer — start with the anatomy of a flow for the core mental model.

tags/projects/games/index.title: #games
tags/projects/games/index.content: While I don’t actively develop any games at this point, it’s always been something in my orbit. Projects that either are games, or related to games, will crop up here.

tags/projects/games/magic-atlas/index.title: #magic-atlas
tags/projects/games/magic-atlas/index.content: A data engineering project utilizing Flowthru to perform and display analytics related to the card game Magic: The Gathering. Uses .NET for the data analytics pipelines, and TypeScript for the associated site and MCP server.

tags/projects/games/roblox/index.title: #roblox
tags/projects/games/roblox/index.content: In late highschool and early college, I did a bit of work with my family on developing and maintaining games on the site Roblox. It’s something on my radar, but not likely to come up again in the near future.

tags/projects/games/the-neighborhood/ind.title: #the-neighborhood
tags/projects/games/the-neighborhood/ind.content:
The Neighborhood is a concept for a game that is still coming together in my head. I consider it to be, to some extent, an video game adaptation the 1977 urban design manual A Pattern Language.
Once I have more details on the project, those will be tagged here.

tags/projects/homelab/index.title: #homelab
tags/projects/homelab/index.content: One of my hobbies is taking old computers and spinning them up as servers in my home. All of these posts are related to running home servers.

tags/projects/index.title: #projects
tags/projects/index.content: I’m a person who likes to package up my work and slap a bow on it, so a lot of what I do will be framed as projects. Some of these may be literal repositories of code within my personal and CGC GitHub organizations. Other work — particularly around data analytics and visualizations and economics research — will be published here.

tags/projects/site/index.title: #site
tags/projects/site/index.content:
#projects/site is a tag dedicated to the mechanical work done on this website. In general, this site is grown up in two places:

The writing and note-taking portions of this vault are managed with Obsidian, a fantastic notes app; and
The site — which takes the notes and publishes them — utilizes a version of the Quartz framework with heavy TypeScript modifications for things like widgets and easier graph customizations.

My goal is to grow out the site itself to better fit the style and content I’m aiming for, in order to build it into a better system for recording my thoughts and making the bearable ones publicly available. As I work more on Quartz, as well as mechanical customizations to Obsidian, any related notes will be published here.

tags/projects/teaching/index.title: #teaching
tags/projects/teaching/index.content: For most of college, I worked in a few different jobs teaching math and programming to kids from grades 2 to 12 (as well as some college tutoring). I also had a few side roles doing professional development and job prep for undergrad students. As those guides continue to crop up, they’ll show up here.

tags/projects/undergrad/index.title: #undergrad
tags/projects/undergrad/index.content: In 2022, I graduated with an undergraduate degree in Quantitative Analysis of Markets and Organizations (it’s just economics with a fancy name) and Computer Science. The start of this blog and the end of the degree overlapped a bit — any of those posts will be marked here.

tags/writing/annotations/a-pattern-langu.title: #a-pattern-language
tags/writing/annotations/a-pattern-langu.content:
#a-pattern-language is a collection of notes and annotations about A Pattern Language (by C. Alexander, S. Ishikawa, M. Silverstein et al.), a manual published in 1977 setting up a design language for urban planning and development.
I would highly recommend this book! It’s an all-around great read about how to better understand the physical spaces we all live and work in. Even if you have no interest in urban planning and development, the book is still a fantastic read for software engineers (or any other engineer, really): it was the inspiration for the style and layout of the seminal object-oriented programming guide Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software, and can help you be a better architect, engineer, and communicator.
You can find A Pattern Language:

Online at PatternLanguage.com
As a partial PDF copy through Cornell University.
A (beautiful!) online index of the overall structure, created by Jenn Scheer.


This is closely tied to another project, The Neighborhood, that I’ve been mulling over for a few years, now. A Pattern Language is large part of the research portion of The Neighborhood — you can find the kickoff and connection in Pattern Languages & The Neighborhood.

tags/writing/annotations/index.title: #annotations
tags/writing/annotations/index.content: Occasionally, the notes on this site will be annotative notes on other folks’ works that I find interesting. Whenever possible, I’ll make these annotations public, especially when the sources are publicly available.

tags/writing/articles/index.title: #articles
tags/writing/articles/index.content: #writing/articles contains notes that have gone through a stricter editorial process. Of all the notes in this vault, I expect these to be for more general audiences, and to be more helpful than other, less-refined writing.

tags/writing/highlights/index.title: #highlights
tags/writing/highlights/index.content: The #highlights category is dedicated to notes that are generally timeless, either because they talk about subjects that aren’t rapidly changing or because I plan on keeping them updated for longer periods of time as new information becomes available.

tags/writing/index.title: #writing
tags/writing/index.content:
One of my many hopes from maintaining this site is to improve my own writing, hopefully developing a distinct voice over time in this era of AI-generated, slop content.
Readers beware — the further back you go, the cringier it’ll get.

tags/writing/tutorials/index.title: #tutorials
tags/writing/tutorials/index.content: Whenever I do work that feels like it would be broadly helpful to others, I’ll place it under the #writing/tutorials tag. These posts will go through a bit more formal review than other notes to make sure that they’re genuinely helpful.
